title: Connexions de Gauss-Manin et équations de Picard-Fuchs. Opération de Cartier : copies de tapuscrit annoté (s.d.), tiré à part (1981), notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Context (pp. 133-135). Grothendieck gives an algebraic definition of projective connections on a smooth relative curve X/S. Write ω = Ω^1_{X/S}.

(1) Torsor structure (previous page). Projective structures on X/S correspond bijectively to order-3 lifts of a certain jet datum. They form a torsor 𝒞_{X/S} under Hom(ω, ω^{⊗3}) ≅ ω^{⊗2}. Equivalently they are connections on the associated P^1-bundle P = P(E), or on its rank-3 Lie algebra bundle V ≅ Sym^2E ⊗ ω^{-1}. V is a successive extension of ω, O, ω^{-1}, and the connections must satisfy a normalisation condition on the sub-line ω ⊂ V.

(2) This page: the normalisation. The relevant extension of ω by ω⊗Ω^1 ≅ ω^2 is canonically the bundle of first principal parts P^1_{X/S}(ω). The condition is that the connection restricted to ω ⊂ V is the universal first-order differential operator d^1 : ω → P^1_{X/S}(ω). This is the oper/'Griffiths transversality with identity graded piece' condition. Grothendieck then checks the bookkeeping. One might expect the residual freedom to live in a group depending on V. Instead it lives in ω⊗Ω^1 ≅ ω^{⊗2}, recovering the torsor group of step (1) ('on retombe sur ses pattes').

(3) Application, S = Spec C. Take X a smooth (possibly affine) complex curve. The transcendental construction recalled earlier is presumably Fuchsian/Koebe uniformization, i.e. the developing map to P^1 modulo PSL_2. Grothendieck reinterprets it as a canonical section of the torsor 𝒞_{X/C} of projective connections. In other words, a canonical P^1-bundle connection on P_X ≅ P(I/I^3), where I is the augmentation ideal of P^∞_{X/S} and I/I^3 is the rank-2 bundle of 2-jets, an extension of ω by ω^2.

(4) Question posed. Does this canonical projective connection have 'logarithmic poles', i.e. regular singularities at the points at infinity of X?

(5) Next page. The answer is that the section extends to the compactification X̂ with at most simple poles along D = X̂ − X, so the indeterminacy group becomes H^0(X̂, ω^2(D)). The exact sequence 0 → H^0(ω^2) → H^0(ω^2(D)) → H^0(D, ω|D) → 0 (for g ≥ 2) is then matched with cotangent spaces of M_g and M_{g,ν}. This is the classical identification of T*M_{g,n} with quadratic differentials having at most simple poles. The direction suggests viewing the uniformization section as varying over moduli, the uniformization projective connection as a family over M_{g,ν}.
errors: Gap/imprecision: regular singularity ('logarithmic poles') of a projective connection at a puncture only forces the difference with a regular-singular reference to have at most double poles; it lies in ω^2(2D), not ω^2(D). At most simple poles additionally fixes the leading coefficient, i.e. the local exponents (exponent difference 0, the cusp/parabolic case realized by Fuchsian uniformization). So the next page's 'pôles simples au plus' and indeterminacy group H^0(ω^2(D)) are correct for the class of uniformization-type (cuspidal) projective connections, not for all regular-singular ones. The page does not make this distinction explicit.
The phrase 'sauf erreur' shows Grothendieck himself flagged the regular-singularity criterion as unverified.

ideas.what: Algebraic definition of projective connections on a relative curve as a torsor under ω^{⊗2}, via jets / P(I/I^3) / P^1-bundle connections with the oper normalisation by the universal differential operator d^1: ω → P^1(ω)
ideas.modern_name: projective connections / sl_2-opers (algebraic definition via principal parts)
ideas.where_published: Not in EGA/SGA as far as I know; this cote's notes are unpublished

ideas.what: Uniformization of a complex curve viewed as a canonical section of the torsor of projective connections
Regular singularity / simple-pole behaviour of the uniformizing projective connection at cusps; indeterminacy H^0(ω^2(D)) identified with T*M_{g,ν}
ideas.modern_name: cusp behaviour of the Fuchsian projective connection; cotangent space of M_{g,n} as quadratic differentials with simple poles
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical Teichmüller theory (Ahlfors, Bers); Zograf-Takhtajan for the moduli variation

missed.claim: By casting Fuchsian uniformization as a canonical section of the algebraic torsor 𝒞 of projective connections, Grothendieck sets up (next page) the comparison with cotangent spaces of M_g and M_{g,ν}. This prefigures viewing the uniformization section over moduli as a non-holomorphic section of an affine bundle modelled on T*M_{g,n}. That is the framework of Zograf-Takhtajan (1987), where the ∂̄ of the section gives the Weil-Petersson form and differences of sections are ∂ of the Liouville action. It is also the setting for the accessory-parameter problem. Only the set-up is present here, not the results.
missed.quote: s'interprète comme la construction d'une connexion projective (canonique) sur X/C, i.e. d'une section canonique ... du torseur des connexions projectives sur X
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historically interesting as an early algebraic framing (1970s) of the uniformization projective connection inside a Gauss-Manin/Picard-Fuchs project. It is mathematically not new.

deep.surprise_reason: The content is a careful algebraic set-up of projective connections (essentially opers) and the classical observation that the uniformization projective structure has cusp-type regular singularities. Both are well known. The only mildly notable point is Grothendieck's framing of uniformization as a torsor section linked to moduli cotangent spaces, foreshadowing later work. It is not developed here.
transcription_corrections: The torsor on this page is written as script C, i.e. $\mathcal{C}_{X/\mathbb{C}}$ (consistent with the previous page's $\mathcal{C}_{X/S}$), not $\mathcal{P}_{X/\mathbb{C}}$.
Line 4 reads 'à l'op. diff. de degré 1 (rel. à S) universel sur ω' — 'universel' is correct.
The indeterminacy line seems to read '(covariant avec V par produit, i.e. dans V⊗ω)' and 'Γ(ω⊗V)'. The dual sign ∨ is doubtful.
The left-margin vertical text is largely illegible. It mentions 'connexion', 'P^∞' and 'singularités régulières', with a bracketed note near the bottom referencing $\mathbb{P}$ and 'Grothendieck'?
